speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43 does, indeed, concern a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of recent actions by the United States government which appear to limit entry to U.S. lands adjacent or close to the Alaska-Canada border, especially in the Panhandle region, and in view of the fact that access to these lands is essential for resource exploration in northern British Columbia and the Yukon, I ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen):
That the Government of Canada investigate the effect of the U.S. land withdrawals on mineral and other resource development on affected Canadian lands and that the government move promptly to preserve the right of unimpeded access through the Alaska border which were granted to Canada in 1825 under the Russo-British Treaty and later reconfirmed in 1903 under the Alaska Boundary Treaty between Canada and the United States.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

This House has a right to know if an act which it passed in good faith is going to be consistently frustrated by the Government of Canada. Since the minister can expect that he would get that agreement from the House of Commons, will he seek the agreement to take the extraordinary procedure of tabling the legal opinion of the Government of Canada so we will know what future assaults there might be upon the Human Rights Act?

MR. DICK-LOTO CANADA-PRESIDENT'S REPORT INTO LOTO SELECT PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to raise a question of privilege of which I have given you notice, and notice to the minister involved. The point arises out of a motion under Standing Order 43 which I put on June 26, 1978, and to which the minister replied in a letter dated June 28, 1978. In the letter signed by the minister in ink, in her own hand I believe, it states:
This letter is in reference to your question under Standing Order 43 made Friday, June 23, 1978. I will send you a letter received from Loto Canada concerning the letting of a three year contract to General Instrument (Canada) Limited.
There are two other paragraphs which do not pertain to this, asking whether I wanted a briefing and so on. The letter which I was then sent is dated June 26, 1978, and is signed by Mr. Cousineau, the president of Loto Canada.
I have had to go through an awful lot of correspondence as well as a report which was filed in this House on February 21 to make sure there was accuracy and that I would not be bringing up what may be an error in a question of privilege. There has been much checking and verification. I believe this is an important question of privilege; there are many anomalies, contradictions and oversights in the report which was tabled on Wednesday, February 21, as a report from the president of Loto Canada. Generally, the report follows a number of order paper questions which I had put down, starting at No. 1,030. It certainly does not go into the matter in any detail as I had requested.
The Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mrs. Campagnolo) tabled in the House a document which she said constituted a report of Loto Canada to her regarding the resolution of contracts having to do with the abandoned Loto Select games. I served notice immediately that Appendix B in the table of documents which purports to be a copy of a letter sent by Guy Cousineau, the president of Loto Canada, to the minister on June 26, 1978, is in fact not that letter.
On June 28 of last year the minister sent to me a letter signed by herself in which she enclosed a photocopy of the letter of June 26, 1978, signed by Guy Cousineau. The letter the minister tabled is, in fact, an altered version, and a significant paragraph has been deleted.

subtopic: MR. DICK-LOTO CANADA-PRESIDENT'S REPORT INTO LOTO SELECT PROJECT
speechtext: Oh!

subtopic: MR. DICK-LOTO CANADA-PRESIDENT'S REPORT INTO LOTO SELECT PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the nineteenth edition of Erskine May states clearly on page 141, under the title "Presenting Forged, Falsified or Fabricated Documents to Either House or Committees of Either House":
It is a breach of privilege to present or cause to be presented to either House or to committees of either House forged, falsified or fabricated documents with intent to deceive such House or committees or to subscribe the names of other persons or fictitious names to documents intended to be presented-
I am not suggesting that a wrong name has been added or that a name has been forged, but I am saying it is a fabricated document. Under the next heading on the same page, "Conspiracy to Deceive Either House or Committees of Either House," we read:
-persons who present false, forged or fabricated documents to either House or to committees of either House are guilty of a breach of privilege.
Under the third heading on that page, "Abstracting or Altering Documents Presented to the House", Erskine May
states:
To abstract any record or other document from the custody of the Clerk or to falsify or improperly alter any records of, or documents presented to either House, or committees of either House, will constitute a contempt.
As I have stated, on June 28 the minister sent me a covering letter, which I have read in part, together with a copy of a letter from Mr. Cousineau to herself dated June 26 outlining the circumstances surrounding Loto Canada's computer game, Loto Select. Now I find in the report tabled by the minister, half way down page seven, the following:
With no time available to eliminate problems after commencement only proven performance was considered acceptable. Potential performance or hypothetical capability would constitute an unacceptable risk as prejudicing either credibility and/or time limits. (This topic is dealt with at somewhat greater length in the letter contained in Appendix B of June 26, 1978).
Now I find that in the report tabled by the minister there exists this Appendix B which purports to be a letter dated June 26, 1978, from Mr. Cousineau to herself. I would draw the attention of the House to the fact that this letter as tabled appears to have been altered and subsequently signed, with a few changes in punctuation-a few commas have been added or deleted as is normal, I guess, when retyping. The margins have been reset, and starting at the bottom of page two of the letter they shift one paragraph over to the top of page three, so you start to get caught up when they delete the paragraph.
Page one is identical, word for word and paragraph for paragraph, as between the two versions. Page two begins with a paragraph saying: "Accordingly, following from the second of the foregoing-" and ends, in the last sentence, "In the circumstances, I believe this attitude on our part was both necessary and justified." On the other hand, the letter which was sent to me dated June 26 started on page two with the words: "Accordingly, following from the second of the foregoing points-", words identical to those in the other letter, but there is another paragraph on that page; in the tabled version that paragraph has been slipped over to the top of page three and everything slides down a little bit. So it gets to be on page three, and a paragraph is missing.
On page three of the original letter of June 26, a copy of which I left with your office, Mr. Speaker, on serving notice, there is a paragraph which states:
On balance, therefore, and keeping in mind that the tendering process alone would consume between three and four months of the limited pre-1980 time

February 28, 1979

period, the corporation judged that it was fully justified in entering into a sole-sourced contract.
Considering that much of the debate has been concerned with tendering, or lack of tendering, and the sole sourcing of a large contract directed to an American firm, it is odd that that paragraph should have been omitted in its entirety from the version tabled in the House of Commons on Wednesday last. It was a key paragraph of the original letter. In it, the president of the corporation outlined Loto Canada's reasons for sole-sourcing this important and costly contract to an American firm. Yet in the document tabled in the House the paragraph has been deleted, and the letter signed again by the president of Loto Canada as if it had been the letter of January 26, 1978. All other paragraphs and words in the two versions are identical. Mr. Speaker, I believe this constitutes a prima facie case of privilege.
I should also like to state that there are other anomalies in the document tabled by the minister which contradict previous statements made by her in the House and which would, it seems to me, lead to the conclusion that the hon. lady has misled the House at least on occasions in relation to Loto Select. I feel that this alteration of a document before it was tabled constitutes such a flagrant breach of privilege that it should immediately be brought to the attention of the House. Should Your Honour find that a prima facie question of privilege has been established, on the basis of the references I have made to Erskine May and other authorities, I would be prepared to move:
That the tabling in the House of Commons on Wednesday February 21, by the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport of a report on the circumstances surrounding Loto Canada's computer game Loto Select, a part of which was a letter, Appendix B, which purports to be a copy of the letter sent by the president of Loto Canada to the minister on June 26, 1978 regarding Loto Select, but in fact which is a significantly altered version of that letter, be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

The hon. member did not know of the alleged anomalies and omissions when he called my office today. He did not know them yesterday when he raised this, so I have not been accorded the privilege of knowing whatever prior knowledge he may have had of what it was he was going to bring forward today.
We know that the prime matter to be brought forward is whether there was an attempt to deceive. This is the essential element which has been brought forward by the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick).

However, the hon. member once again today raised the question of what he has referred to as the American purchase. In this regard I can say that the hon. member himself was guilty of irresponsible and reprehensible behaviour when he attended the Ontario unveiling of a software purchase and said that it was an all-Canadian purchase. The fact is that the Ontario Lottery is and was as dependent upon American software as was Loto Canada at that time. The hon. member has raised this repeatedly in the House, and he has done so again today, so I would like to address myself to that.
The Ontario and Quebec games are so dependent on American software that the most recent edition of an American trade publication contains an article, which I want to table today, entitled "Datatrol Inc. of Hudson Massachusetts' new programmable wagering terminal" which says, and I quote:
The first installations of this terminal took place last November in the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Quebec under the direction of the Ontario Lottery Corporation and Loto Quebec.
The hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton has repeatedly said that Loto Canada's decision to lease from an American subsidiary was a wrongful act, and he based this assertion on the fact that Ontario was able to make purchases in like manner from a Canadian corporation which, in fact, it did not. That is demonstrated in the documents which I table herewith.
The hon. member referred to some fine phrases by opposition members from time to time. He has in fact backed the Canadian computer industry, which I think is commendable. However, the fact is that last year the Canadian computer industry did not yet have the capability to develop an integrated gaming system of the kind required by Loto Select as well as by Ontario and Quebec. It is because of this, and because of Loto Canada's desire in its capacity as a Crown corporation to support the government's over-all industrial strategy, that Loto Canada has initiated through the Department of Supply and Services a research granting system of up to $500,000 in order to develop Canadian production of gaming and lottery technology programs.
The hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton castigated me in his news conference for having been the minister responsible for a corporation which leased from an American company, but he himself was false when he made-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, looking ahead to the defence which will be offered I just want to indicate that it is our view-and I say this with respect-that the question raised by the minister as to whether there was an intent to deceive is not a question with respect to the matter of privilege. That is a question for the committee to decide. That is a matter which goes to the committee. The question before the House is whether there was a discrepancy between two documents. It is a question of a discrepancy, by omission, between the two documents. That is an assertion which has been made, and I think when the minister returns to the House she should direct herself to that point, bearing in mind the principle Your Honour set out in a lengthy and, I think, very learned and acceptable judgment involving the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) where that was the precise issue.
That is the question, and that is the matter upon which I presume Your Honour would find that there is a prima facie case. The matter would then go to the committee, assuming that a majority of the members of this House voted to send it to the committee. That was the issue in the case of the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham. That is the matter about which my hon. friend opposite is grunting. In that case the government voted against the openness which this House wanted with respect to that question.
The last matter is that it might be helpful to the House if, in anticipation of what the minister is going to say, and dealing with the narrow question which the House must consider-as to whether there are any other documents which ought to be tabled-perhaps the minister could undertake now to table in advance of her argument-perhaps later today when we would be prepared to give her consent-any other documents, the contracts particularly, to which she is referring, because that is the matter which is of interest to the country. I know the minister smiles a lot, but that is a matter which is of interest to

the country, and if the minister could undertake to disclose the whole of the position taken by the government with respect to this matter, it would be a most refreshing undertaking from this government, and particularly from this minister.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege concerning remarks of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Abbott) yesterday related to my motion under Standing Order 43 on income tax returns of some Red Deer constituents included with those found in boxes in an Ottawa building, unguarded and without adequate security. Every member of parliament is responsible to his or her constituents, and part of that duty is to act on their behalf. Surely no member of this House is to be denied the right to protect those who elected him, particularly involving confidential information entrusted to the Minister of National Revenue.
The general public understandably does not, or has not up until now, been concerned about legislation authorizing or compelling the minister to release income tax returns to another department or agency of government. When they file income tax returns, they are obeying and complying with a federal law.
The minister said in his question of privilege yesterday:
I take exception to the hon. members being able to communicate to the public at large that Revenue Canada does not guard its income tax returns with great care.
February 28, 1979

Had the income tax files in question been "guarded", I would not have moved my motion yesterday. I might add that the boxes with the income tax returns in question were shown on television, giving them far wider publicity and greater impact than verbal representations within this chamber.
The purpose of my motion was to have the Minister of National Revenue communicate with those persons whose files were released to Statistics Canada to reassure them, and to explain how their income tax returns are being used. If the minister accedes to my request, any adverse effect or doubt as a result of the unguarded confidential files could be satisfactorily resolved, at least to a degree.
I take exception to the implication of the Minister of National Revenue that my motion was an attempt to publicize in any way the boxes of unattended and unprotected income tax returns. Surely the minister, the custodian of millions of income tax returns containing perhaps more personal and confidential detail than those of any other federal department, would not find my request unreasonable or unparliamentary.
By exercising a small degree of co-operation, understanding and tolerance, and by accepting the responsibility of his portfolio, the Minister of National Revenue could regain the confidence of the general public, at the same time reassuring this House and Canadians everywhere that confidential information is protected, or will be in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order in reply to a matter raised by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) on February 20, 1979, as an item under routine proceedings. The hon. member questioned replies given to him on question No. 679 on the order paper and in a letter dated February 13, 1979, both of which concerned the RCMP Highway Detachment Building located at Steinbach, Manitoba. The reply to the question on the order paper was signed by my parliamentary secretary, and the letter was signed by myself.
The hon. member for Provencher alleged that there was a discrepancy between the answers given to him. I have taken the opportunity of reviewing question No. 679 on the order paper and the correspondence. Question No. 679 asked if the government is planning expansion of the RCMP Highway Detachment Building located at Steinbach, Highway No. 12, and its response was "No". There are no proposals to expand that building. However, as indicated in the letter to the hon. member for Provencher, interior renovations, as well as a new parking lot at the rear of the building, are programmed for the fiscal year 1980-81. I do not consider there is a conflict in the response to question No. 679 vis-a-vis the letter sent to the hon. member. As hon. members opposite word their questions on the order paper with care, the answers also are worded carefully with reference to the questions asked.

Mr. Speaker, the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) was correct in outlining the case. It was pretty well a repeat of what I raised on February 20 as reported at pages Nos. 3412 and 3413 of Hansard.
In the technical sense the minister said I used the word "expand" the detachment building in Steinbach, namely, the rural detachment located on Highway No. 12. The minister made the claim, if I understand him correctly, that if the physical dimensions of the building are not expanded, the square footage of the building, then the building is not expanded. If I interpret him correctly, then the government answered my question correctly by a negative answer of "No". But the minister knows that in "D" Division headquarters in Winnipeg, as well as at RCMP detachment offices in Steinbach, for some time there have been discussions on renovating the building. In the manner in which the question was asked, it was quite clear I was asking for the building program for that detachment building. Now the minister claims that it is not being expanded but in fact they will go forward with the renovations as had been discussed by the RCMP in the various forms which I have mentioned.
While the minister, in the very technical sense and with a dictionary definition of "expansion", might be able to get away with a negative answer, the fact of the matter is that it was a question requesting information on behalf of my constituents.
February 28, 1979
You won't get that from them.

What I did get was a totally wrong impression and my constituents got a totally wrong impression that the building project which had been purported to go forward, now was not to go forward. Most hon. members in the House who come from rural areas recognize that if a federal building project is to take place in their area, there is a lot of discussion in the concerned area before the project ever gets under way. There is extreme interest in local rural areas as to whether the federal government will go forward with the project. In this case it was an RCMP detachment building.
Members of the force are very close members of the community and they speak with other members of the community. The impression left was that the government planned to go forward with renovations. But when I received a "No" answer to my written question, the impression was that the project was dead. A few days later I received the minister's answer in letter form arguing that the project was to go forward again. I could stand here a long time arguing whether a parking lot attached to a detachment building is expansion or renovation. I do not know what is being renovated, but I know what is being expanded. Now that the minister is trying to hide behind the words "expansion" and "renovation", I hope this case will be put to rest only on the basis that he will go forward with the expansion and/or renovations which were planned a long time ago.

subtopic: ENERGY SUPPLIES EMERGENCY ACT, 1979 MEASURES TO CONSERVE STOCKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill we are dealing with today concerning emergency powers to be given the government to allocate energy in the event of an interruption or dislocation of supply, is one of tremendous importance, and we want to make a few observations before it moves to the committee.
One has to ask oneself how many energy crises we, as a country, will have to face before this government takes action in terms of implementing a rational energy policy geared to the goal of self-sufficiency in energy for consumers in Canada. What brought on this most recent example of the need for a bill is in everyone's mind, namely, the Iranian situation whereby some 100,000 barrels of oil usually destined for Canada were cut off because of domestic problems in Iran. What happened to make the situation worse, of course, was a deci-

February 28, 1979
Energy Supplies
sion by the Exxon oil company of the United States in a directive to its Canadian subsidiary, Imperial Oil, to divert some 25,000 barrels of crude from Venezuela bound for Canada. Of course this made the situation for the people in eastern Canada all the more precarious.
I do not have to remind the Elouse that back in 1973 and 1974 we faced a similar crisis when world supply was, or appeared to be, interrupted, and the Liberal government at that time brought forward an emergency bill to give it the necessary powers to deal with rationing and other procedures needed in Canada. Unfortunately, at the insistence of the Conservative party, there was a time limit. The measure was to expire after two years, and it did so, I believe in 1976. As a result we have to go through the whole process again of re-introducing and passing a similar bill.
The passage of this one bill really does not go to the root of the problem, the real vulnerability of Canada in terms of energy. Because of the government's lack of initiative, and because of the backward looking policies of previous Liberal and Conservative governments, we are in a situation today where a country such as Canada, which in theory should be self-sufficient in energy needs, is in reality dependent upon imported oil from OPEC countries to meet consumer needs east of the Ottawa valley. That shortsighted policy of not building an oil pipeline from our western Canadian oil fields to our east coast has now caught up with us on two very dramatic occasions. This indicates the real powerlessness of the Canadian government without the option of Canadian supply for Canadian markets.
When we recall that over 90 per cent of our oil industry is foreign owned it soon becomes apparent that the options the government has to implement energy policy in the interest of Canadians are limited, indeed. When Imperial Oil got the order from its parent company, Exxon, that once again pointed out dramatically how we are at the mercy of the multinational oil companies. We do not have an energy policy stressing Canadian self-sufficiency and Canadian control of our energy resources.
We in this party have argued time and time again, in this House and elsewhere, from the earliest days of the 1960s, that we must have public control and ownership of our vital energy sector if we are to develop a nation that is economically strong, and if we are to be in a position to avoid the kind of precariousness of supply and the kind of blackmail that can take place as a result of decisions by OPEC or the multinationals.
We had a spectacle just a few weeks ago when Imperial announced it was going to divert Venezuelan oil bound for Canada to other markets of the Exxon corporation in order to make up for the shortfall that Exxon was experiencing in its other markets because of the Iranian cutback. We had the spectacle of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Gillespie) begging the subsidiary of a multinational oil company, Imperial Oil, to please not divert the oil that was regularly bound for

Canada, contracted under due legal process for the Canadian market.
Indeed, that situation is still not resolved. Imperial has cut down on the amount of oil it wanted to divert, but this does not go to the root of the problem; nor does it offer us as consumers a long-range solution to the problems resulting from an interruption of supply.
Surely we, as Canadians, need no further evidence that we have to reverse this disastrous energy policy pursued by this Liberal government if we are to proceed on a sound and rational basis for the supply of energy in this country. When we consider the way out we know it is not, as the Conservatives would have it, just to leave it all to the private sector in the hope that somehow, through private initiative and private decision making, there will be enough oil found to meet our needs for decades to come. That is just not going to work. Surely the oil crisis we saw in the middle 1970s, and the oil crisis we see now, are evidence of the fact that the situation has gone beyond the control of the multinationals or private energy companies. Therefore the only way we, as a country, can stop that kind of blackmail, that threat and that lack of control, is to have the Government of Canada as a public authority begin to take an active role in energy policy-making in this country.
The private oil companies have no loyalty but to themselves. They are part of a multinational oil conglomerate, and they have interests which have no loyalty to any one country, but only to the over-all global plan of the multinational itself. If we are to avoid future situations, such as where a multinational like Exxon tells its Canadian subsidiary, Imperial, to do this or that-irrespective of what it means to Canadian policy-we must have public ownership and control of our energy sector.
We do have an option, and as a result of the policies that the New Democratic Party was able to pressure this government into taking during the minority parliament of 1972-1974 and during the energy crisis of those years when we held the balance of power, action which it would not have taken if it were in a majority situation, because the Liberals are just as wedded to the free enterprise ideal in the oil industry as are the Conservatives, now, however, we have Petro-Canada, the national oil company owned by the people of Canada through their federal government.
This company can provide us with an option to the kind of dominance by the multinationals in our energy sector. When Petro-Canada was set up we advocated that it take an active role in the beginning to buy back our energy resources so that we would have Canadian ownership and, hence, some Canadian decision-making authority in the field of energy in this country.
It was a very slow start under the Liberal government once it was returned with a majority in 1974, and Petro-Canada did not move in a big way into the energy market. I think, though, that the government has seen the logic of our argument, and it now realizes that one way we can get out of the current
February 28, 1979

dilemma is for Petro-Canada to play a larger role in our oil industry. This current crisis presents us, therefore, with an excellent opportunity to use our national, public petroleum company in a positive and progressive manner, and that is to avoid the kind of blackmail situation or arbitrary decision making taken by the multinational parent companies. Instead of Exxon dictating to Imperial or through Imperial to arrange the contracts for supply, the way out is to use Petro-Canada as the sole agency for arranging oil contracts with producing nations.
We know that the government of Venezuela is quite anxious to negotiate supply contracts on a government-to-government basis. Venezuela, of course, is the major supplier of oil to eastern Canada, since we do not have a pipeline from the west. Surely this is a golden opportunity for Petro-Canada to act as sole agent for purchasing all the oil which Venezuela is willing to sell to Canada. In this way we can avoid the kind of stranglehold position which Exxon has over supply from Venezuela. If Petro-Canada were the sole purchasing agent- and it would be a paper transaction since Petro-Canada does not have the tankers to move the oil-then it could farm out to the subsidiary companies in Canada the oil destined for Canadian markets. This is a short-term, interim solution to the problems we are facing now.
In the long term, of course, the real solution would be to establish a system which would preclude any subsidiary of a multinational oil company from dominating the market and being able to interrupt energy supply or cause an energy crisis to escalate, contrary to the interests of the Government of Canada. Our party has advocated for some years now that Petro-Canada buy out Canada's largest oil company, Imperial Oil, the leader in oil and energy decision making in this country, so that the Crown corporation could be the leader in the oil industry in terms of exploration decisions, supply decisions, and price decisions.
We know that Petro-Canada has bought out Pacific Petroleums but, again, it is not the major company. We still have a long way to go in order to control or break the stranglehold which the multinationals have on our energy sector. It appalls me to listen in this House to the Conservative party's answer to the dilemma we are in now. Of course, they would have us dismantle Petro-Canada, our only national oil company, and sell it back to the private sector. This would leave us right back at square one and in the kind of dilemma in which we now find ourselves.
If we do not have an option to the multinational companies in terms of a national, publicly controlled oil company, then we have no bargaining tool or policy at our disposal to reverse this dangerous trend which has developed. Surely Canadians who are concerned about pricing and supply should reject the policy of the Conservative party and make it known to them that their policy to abolish Petro-Canada is unacceptable and that it would work against the interest of all Canadians. If we are to have a national energy policy we need initiatives now to deal with an emergency should it arise, not just in terms of this bill, but some long-range plans, because energy is not only
Energy Supplies
related to heating our homes or driving our automobiles, it is related to the whole manufacturing and industrial sector of our economy.
Think of the advantages, Mr. Speaker, we could have had as a nation if we had initiated a policy for national interests rather than relying on the multinational oil companies. Think of the advantages we could have had in terms of avoiding the kind of price increases that the OPEC nations were able to impose on North America. If Canada has an enlightened policy of public development of our oil supplies we would have a pipeline from east to west. We could have been self-sufficient in oil and avoided the kind of price escalation when oil quadrupled in price over a few years. Because the multinational oil companies did not want a pipeline built to eastern Canada, because they were more interested in developing our western reserves for export to the American market, we have had to rely on Middle East and Venezuelan oil for eastern Canada. Once the OPEC nations pushed up the price of that oil, eastern Canada had to pay the higher price and, as a result, the price was forced up in western Canada. But that is an old story and one that I need not go into because I think most members in this House are well aware of it.
We must not react from crisis to crisis by introducing measures such as we have before the House today. We have to use public instruments, such as Petro-Canada and legislation in terms of regaining control, to implement a policy of self-sufficiency in oil and natural gas or that will bring us as close as possible to that goal. This means, of course, extending the pipeline from Montreal to eastern Canada to provide oil eventually for that market, especially when the tar sands production comes on stream. It also means that we must reduce our exports of oil to the United States. We have exported so much of our oil that we now face shortages in the long term. We should be implementing a policy of storage of oil in some of the abandoned mines in Newfoundland and the maritime provinces so that we are not caught short. We should be looping the Sarnia to Montreal pipeline so that we can deliver more oil to the Montreal area in the event of interruptions or cutbacks in supply to eastern Canada.
Surely one of the things which we must look at with renewed interest and some urgency, to displace our dependence on imported oil in Atlantic Canada, is natural gas. That, of course, means extending the natural gas pipeline to the maritime provinces. That is an important goal. The government has expressed some interest in doing so. But I do not see the kinds of initiatives needed now to give some kind of relief to the poor consumer in Atlantic Canada who is paying outrageous prices for oil. We could displace some of that oil needed by extending a natural gas pipeline, because natural gas currently is priced at 85 per cent of the price of oil. That leads me to what is taking place this afternoon. The National Energy Board in an hour or so will release its decision concerning whether we will export more of our natural gas from western Canada to the United States.

subtopic: ENERGY SUPPLIES EMERGENCY ACT, 1979 MEASURES TO CONSERVE STOCKS
speechtext:
From all reports that we see in this morning's press, from the reports and the predictions it would appear that we will see once more western Canadian natural gas exported to the United States. I quote from an article which appeared in this morning's Globe and Mail written by Jeff Carruthers. He says:
The National Energy Board has decided that there is a sufficient surplus of western Canadian gas to support new short-term exports of slightly more than 600 million cubic feet a day over 15 years or almost 1 billion cubic feet a day if a shorter, 10-year period is used.
However, to achieve this, the NEB has had to modify its domestic protection formula used to calculate the amount of domestic gas that has to be set aside for "foreseeable" domestic needs, including new eastern markets.
I have not seen the report, which I say is due to be released in detail in a short while, and I have not examined the revision of the formula, but if this report in this morning's press is accurate that the National Energy Board is to allow natural gas exports, the only way it can do so is, as the report said, to revise the formula that declares what is surplus to Canada's needs. The indication is that the National Energy Board, in order to justify these exports, has revised the formula downward. It has given Canadians less protection in terms of what amount of gas should remain in order to meet our future demands. If that is true, it soon becomes quite obvious that the Liberal government is using this situation, and looking at the politics of the situation rather than the energy interests of Canadians. The Liberal government understands that by allowing exports of natural gas to the United States this will in turn have the effect of boosting the value of the Canadian dollar. That is a very important political consideration for this government on the eve of a federal election.
It would seem to me that what is happening here is that in the short term interests of saving the hide of the Liberal party by means of pushing up the value of the dollar by exports of natural gas, that short-term interest has taken precedence over the long-term energy interests of Canadians. That is indeed, Mr. Speaker, a sad commentary on the kind of thinking that goes on in the cabinet. As we know, the cabinet does give direction to the National Energy Board.
Here we are in the middle of an energy crisis approving more natural gas exports to the United States when it is so obvious that we need to ensure future supplies for Canada in this energy sparse world, and it is so obvious that Atlantic Canada needs this natural gas to help offset these high oil prices. Surely any government that had the interests of Canada at heart, instead of thinking of saving its political hide by hoping a short-term policy will boost the value of the Canadian dollar, would realize that we have to protect our future energy needs by ensuring that that natural gas remains in Canada for use by Canadians.
It seems so backward in our thinking that we should be exporting natural gas at this time in our history, especially when there are indications that certain areas of the United States, for example, Texas, have their own gas bubble or surplus. The Americans, I think, are rather shrewd; they prefer to keep their natural gas in the ground and use Canadian gas

because they know what the future holds in terms of energy supplies.
We can only suspect the kind of decision that will be made by the National Energy Board, given its past record. In the past the National Energy Board, by listening to the multinational oil and gas companies, has told Canadians that we have an abundant supply not only of oil but of natural gas, enough natural gas to last us into the 21st century. We have seen how they have been proven wrong by overrelying on the figures which industry supplies to them. Only a short while ago industry was telling us that we would freeze in the dark and if higher prices were not approved new oil and gas would not be found and Canadians would face a disaster.
Suddenly after industry got its high prices, we are now told we have a surplus and we have to export it and get rid of it. Within a year the scenario will be that the industry will be telling us we have a natural gas shortage and that we need higher prices to find new supplies, and the cycle will repeat itself. How many times do we have to be burned by this short-sighted manipulation of figures by the industry, that our National Energy Board swallows holus bolus?
Surely, in the interests of Canadians, we have to oppose any decision at this time by the National Energy Board to export supplies of natural gas to the United States. The assumption that it is surplus to our needs is a false one. I believe that it is being based on a formula which does not look at our energy needs, and indeed, I think the Energy Board is being pressured by the government to allow these exports in the hope that the value of the Canadian dollar will increase and that will look good for the government as it heads into an election.
If we are to define what surplus means, not only must it be in terms of what our projected needs will be according to demand and consumption, but we must be looking at the term surplus in the view of processing more natural gas in Canada to develop a petro-chemical industry in western Canada. If we do that, then the definition of surplus takes on a whole new life. We will then begin to realize that we have to increase the supply of gas even more in Canada to develop a petro-chemical industry and thus provide jobs and dollars for our western provinces.
If we want to supply natural gas to eastern Canada we cannot allow these kinds of huge exports to continue. If we want to develop a petro-chemical industry we must cut back on these natural gas exports. If we want to ensure Canadians will have sufficient supplies of energy down the road, more than just 25 years or ten years' hence, then we must cut back on some of these exports. This can be done without jeopardizing the industry here in Canada.
Many small exploration companies can argue, quite legitimately, that if they cannot export they will suffer cash flow problems. Especially for the smaller companies it would seem to me a wise policy that both provincial and federal governments could buy natural gas and cap it off, leaving it in the ground, because we will need that gas in the future. Saskatchewan did this in the past and it proved a very wise decision. They were able to buy natural gas at six cents per thousand
February 28, 1979

cubic feet. The price today is around $2. That gas is there. It is able to be used by Canadians when they need it. Surely this is the kind of policy we should initiate now to ensure not only sufficient cash flow for the companies but that the gas will be there when we need it.
This whole pressure by the gas industry to export is one of shortsightedness in terms of our long-range energy needs. That has been proven in the past in the way that price and supply have been manipulated. Now we see the proponents of the Alaska natural gas pipeline that is to run through Canada again arguing before a committee of this House that they must prebuild the southern portion of the line in order to finance the eventual whole line that runs to Alaska.
What does that prebuilding mean? It means taking Alberta gas and running it through the southern portion of that line to the United States. In other words, Canadians are financing a natural gas pipeline that we were told in this House had no other purpose but to move Alaska gas to American markets. We will use up our Alberta reserves and export them to the United States at a price of around $2 per thousand cubic feet. We will eventually have to buy back because we will have used up our gas, paying around $4 for Alaska gas. There is no sense to that kind of economic argument other than to maximize the financial position of the natural gas pipeline companies.
The bill before us today, while helping us in terms of an emergency giving this federal government some powers to allocate supply if a crisis comes upon us, does nothing in the long run to solve the very severe energy situation in which this country finds itself because of past misguided policies of both Liberal and Conservative governments. I hope this gives Canadians an opportunity to wake up to the realities of the power of the multinational oil companies in the world today and realize that the only way out is through public ownership and control of our energy sector.

Mr. Speaker, in rising this afternoon I did not think I would have to begin by referring to some of the remarks of the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes), but in view of the nature of them I certainly must do so. The hon. member was completely off base, completely wrong in suggesting that when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) dealt with Imperial Oil about oil supplies for eastern Canada, he was begging, to use the word of the hon. member.
The minister was not begging. He was stating what it was necessary for a company to do, with the firm knowledge that he had the full support of the government behind him in what he was doing. No doubt he had support from certain other parts of the House as well with regard to any action that might have been required to ensure Canada's interests with regard to supply of oil. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources had earlier made arrangements with Venezuela and Mexico, in his usual forward-looking way, to secure oil supplies, and in the best interests of this country he will continue to do that.
Energy Supplies
I am also struck by the fact that the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie liked to make and, in fact, remake a little history, and throw in a few other things to boot. He now thinks that a pipeline should have been built many years ago from central Canada to the Atlantic in order that oil from Alberta and Saskatchewan could be conveyed there. I am not sure that I recall the strength of the argument from any of his friends who lived in those areas of the country at the time the issue was current in that regard.
We developed the policy of building the pipeline to serve up to the Ottawa valley in order to secure supplies by the continued exploration and development of those oil resources in western Canada. We were doing that at some cost in terms of slightly higher oil supplies for this region, justifying that on the basis of security. In other words, in terms of governing policies, we were striking a compromise between the higher costs that had to be paid in the short run and the long-run good of security of supply.
We drew the line against imposing much higher costs for the eastern part of the country which had access to the lowest cost oil available in the world for many, many years. Through that policy we avoided significant additional cost to consumers of oil throughout the whole central and eastern region beyond the Ottawa valley and to the east. At the same time we developed other policies, which the hon. member criticizes, allowing certain exports to the United States so that exploration and development would thereby be encouraged.
I was intrigued by the fact that the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie again criticized us for exporting oil to the United States. He criticized us for not having the oil flow into eastern Canada and the Atlantic, and criticized us for letting it flow to the United States. I understand each of those positions taken separately. However, when he said that because we let it flow to the United States, we disposed of so much oil that we developed for ourselves what he called a long-term shortage, he lost me. If it had flowed to the east instead of the United States, we would be in the same supply situation we are in now. The hon. member cannot have it all three ways. He absolutely cannot.
The hon. member was completely wrong in his analysis. It was typical of what I call eastern NDP members, and by that I mean those from central Canada. He insists that anything we did at that time had to be attributed to some policy or program that was favoured by the oil companies. He said that is why we did not build the pipeline beyond the Ottawa valley.
That is completely wrong. I was minister responsible for energy in 1969. Time and time again I was visited by representatives of the oil companies urging that we move in that direction, urging that the extra cost was worth while in terms of security. They were in favour of that. We were balancing the interests of the people of Canada in terms of lower cost oil available to them at that time. By our additional extension of sales into the United States, we were encouraging the very export and development we now have and which has been very important to us.

I do not know where we would be if we listened to the left and the right with regard to our exports. We would be a fully closed in nation. Just the other day the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) said that we should impose import surcharges, this at a time when the world is trying to move toward freer trade. He finds himself back with the Tories of the nineteenth century. It is clear that Clark's Tories are Tories of the nineteenth century. It is visible in everything they say.
He was going to impose import surcharges. The Tory leader, after criticizing higher prices on goods coming into this country because of the drop in the dollar, was going to impose import surcharges on top of that. Not only that, but he would threaten the whole access we have to the United States market because their balance of payments leaves them to think a little bit about that kind of measure which we must resist in the interests of freer trade.
The NDP, at least those from the east, constantly insist that we not sell anything to the United States. The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie criticized us for selling oil in days gone by to the United States, which was done in order to encourage export and development in Alberta and Saskatchewan. He could not say that honestly and fairly in the face of his friends from the province of Saskatchewan. He discourages us now from exporting gas to the United States.
Just the other day I heard a Conservative spokesman say we should not sell wheat to the Soviet Union. That would be his reaction, he said, for a variety of reasons having to do with certain policies followed by that country. So for one reason or another we would export nothing as a result of positions taken by people from the right or from the left.
The bill before us is important as a consistent part of government policy to make sure we have in place mechanisms to deal with problems of oil and energy. We feel that its early passage is extremely important, and we urge hon. members to make this possible-I understand there is now some agreement that it may go through. The current instability in the Middle East, the problems in Iran, the mobilization of the Saudi Arabian army all make it important that the bill should become law and perhaps justify the comment of the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie that it might have been better had we omitted the sunset clause which now obliges us to spend a great deal of time considering this legislation once again.
Notwithstanding our desire to deal with this matter swiftly, it is important to note that the government's policy with regard to energy has been consistently one of looking ahead, of balancing the interest of obtaining secure supplies against the advantages of access to supplies at as low a cost as possible. Members of the New Democratic Party are caustic, but are they caustic about the fact that we intervened to make sure that prices in Canada would not immediately and in too rapid a fashion reflect the drastic oil price increases which are occurring? Are they caustic about the fact that we have in place pricing mechanisms which mean that the tremendous

potential for price insecurity, the tremendous potential for sudden rises in price, will not have an impact in Canada in any immediate way-that from the Atlantic to the Pacific and, beyond that, to both islands, there are arrangements which secure reasonable prices in this country and provide that only over a gradual period the increases which are going on in the world, and against which we cannot isolate ourselves for ever, will come into effect?
Many have testified to the wisdom of Canadian policy with regard to balancing the various factors involved. Only yesterday before a Senate committee a spokesman for the Northwest Alaskan Pipeline Company, Mr. John G. McMillian, who is also the chief executive officer, was testifying about pipeline and energy matters. Senator Lucien had asked him whether anything on the Canadian side had caused any delay or problem from his point of view. His answer is instructive because, before dealing with that precise question with regard to pipe lines, he said:
No. In fact, we can only compliment you and your government. First, in 1973 when you had an oil crisis you evolved and developed an energy plan that has paid off. Your energy plan is working. You are getting conservation. You have had activity in exploration; you have developed new resources; you are to be complimented on that.
Then he went on to say that we were also to be complimented upon dealing with the pipe line in an expeditious way.

Let us consider Petro-Canada and the important role which was foreseen for it by the government-how completely consistent it is with what the government has done and with what Liberal policy has been over the years in taking action over the years where free enterprise often operates. If I might bring back memories of other voices, that means government action and ownership of private enterprise when necessary, but I will paraphrase slightly and say "only when necessary". I think this states very accurately and very well a good policy for a government of Canada to follow.
The example of Petro-Canada was not brand new. I am talking in particular, really, of its forerunner, of the development of Panarctic and the government's investment in it. I am thinking of the fact that years earlier a majority Liberal government, a government which the hon. member cannot claim to have supported in any way, invested in Panarctic at a time when it was not possible to get private investment to go
February 28, 1979

alone into the risky areas of the north. The Hon. Arthur Laing deserves a great deal of credit for seeing that this was a need which fitted well into the Liberal policy of moving when necessary into areas where private enterprise was not willing or not able to do the job at the time. So this is not a new policy and it does not smack of socialism as the Clark Tories seem to think.
Another example which is consistent with Liberal policy was the creation some 40 years ago of Air Canada. The architect was C, D. Howe, a predecessor of mine, in many ways of whose actions and activities I am very proud. He is not usually thought of as in any way a socialist or as a destroyer of free enterprise. I would recommend to the Clark Tories that they begin to read a little about the philosophy that brought about such a development. At that time, private enterprise was unwilling to produce a Canadian airline. We thought we needed one and therefore we moved to create such an airline so as to serve many communities in this country. That was the only way of getting it. In today's conditions, such action in the aviation field would not have been necessary. But it is necessary now to do something in the area of oil supplies.
Just as, earlier, Panarctic was needed as the explorer in the north and in the Arctic, so Canada needs to acquire additional ownership in a field about which the role and domination of foreign owners has caused so much concern. Petro-Canada has already, in the very short time of its existence, done really great things. The hon. member thinks it has been slow to get off the ground, but in that short period of four years a great deal has been achieved. It is participating now in exploration in Labrador which otherwise would not necessarily be taking place; it has joined in the development of heavy oil projects. Otherwise we might very well have seen a stagnant situation in an area where there is an important need. In bringing Pacific Petroleums to Canadian ownership we made a long-term contribution to our future in oil and oil resources.

That other matter is the position of the Conservative party with relation to whether the federal government should act at all and whether it should play a role with respect to energy resources for Canadians. We have just completed a constitutional conference at which one of the key issues was the position of the federal government on natural resources, and the position to be accorded to the provinces in which those natural resources are found. This federal government reached out as far as it could possibly be expected to reach to find a position which would be satisfactory to provincial interests with regard to provincial ownership, provincial financial rights, and provincial control of the disposition of natural resources in the provinces.
We wrote sections in a proposed draft constitution which effectively gave to the provinces not only recognition of their ownership but also a very full recognition of their place in relation to revenue from these resources. We gave them taxing power, even when that taxing power is indirect in relation to these resources, in the texts we had before us at that conference. We said they could have a good deal of control over distribution, disposition, and exploration of these resources.
Some qualifications were agreed upon. One was that this should not be discriminatory as between provinces in such a way that they could somehow favour one neighbour over another. That was agreed upon. Where the line was drawn was where we felt that there were times when, as a federal government protecting Canadians throughout this country, we needed the ability to legislate in order to ensure that those resources were there for the use of all Canadians. The words we wanted to use as an occasion for our ability to legislate were that we could do so under the federal trade and commerce power when there was a compelling national interest.
Premier Lougheed of Alberta refused to accept that position. Coming from Saskatchewan, I was delighted that Saskatchewan was willing to agree to that. In that regard Mr. Blakeney said at the conference, and I quote:
-and I commend the federal government for their flexibility and their willingness to accommodate in many of these areas.
I would underline that. We for our part came here with the same point of view.
Seeing that we had gone as far as we ought to go at that particular point in time, Premier Lougheed said that he would not accept words which said that a compelling national interest should be a ground for federal legislation, whatever we do in relation to the full control of provinces over their resources.

That must be the role played by a federal government for all of Canada. That is a national role which must be played.

Mr. Speaker, in closing this debate on second reading I should like to say that it has been made very clear in speeches by hon. members opposite and hon. members on this side of the House that we are dealing with a matter of security of supply, security of the Canadian supply, security of the Canadian economy, and security of particular regions of Canada, particularly Atlantic Canada and a large part of Quebec, because,

as hon. members know, that part of the country is dependent on foreign oil for 100 per cent of its supplies.
The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) suggested that the solution to that problem was to build a pipeline down to Atlantic Canada. Perhaps he has forgotten the situation. Perhaps he has forgotten what the National Energy Board had to say about our oil supplies. If he had read those reports, he would have recognized that there has been a significant change for the better as a result of the policies put into place by the government over the last few years.
A little over a year ago the National Energy Board was saying that there was not enough Canadian oil in the west to move through the pipeline, which was built by this government and subsidized by this government, into the Montreal market. That pipeline-which, as I said, is subsidized by the government-is now moving more than 300,000 barrels a day of Canadian crude into the Montreal area. That has reduced our dependence on foreign oil from 800,000 barrels a day to
500,000	barrels a day, very close to a 40 per cent reduction in the level of foreign supplies on which we have to depend. But a little over a year ago the National Energy Board was warning Canadians it would be necessary perhaps to reverse that pipeline, that the oil in the west would not be sufficient to continue moving through the pipeline into Montreal for more than a few years. The early eighties were the time they were suggesting we might have to reverse that pipeline and bring imported oil into the Ontario market.
The last report of the National Energy Board on the oil supply requirements which was issued by them in the past fall indicated that there had been a significant change in the supply situation, that instead of having to contemplate a reversal of the pipeline in a few years, we can now look forward to sustaining the movement of oil from the west to the east. But they also made quite clear that we do not yet have enough oil to contemplate looking after Atlantic Canada from Canadian sources.
Hon. members will know that there is a pipeline in place. But for the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie to suggest, as did the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies), that we should be building a pipeline to the east is to suggest that they have not done their homework, that they are not really familiar with the distribution systems in the country. There is a pipeline from Montreal to Portland which could take Canadian oil down to Portland, Maine, and then by tanker around to the Atlantic ports. There is only one problem at the moment, that is, insufficient oil in place to sustain the movement of oil through that pipeline. That raises one of the really fundamental questions for Canadians that was touched upon very briefly by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in his remarks today.
One of the really basic questions is: How do you ensure security for Canadians when the federal government does not have control over the pace of development of the large western tar sands and the heavy oils of the west? The Minister of Transport referred to compelling national interest and the importance of interpreting this in terms of trade and commerce. I put this question to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES

Clark) and to opposition members: is compelling national interest not going to be a reason for the federal government to consider other measures to ensure the development of the tar sands and the heavy oils? That will be one of the big questions to which Canadians will have to address themselves in the months to come.
There is another aspect of security of supply which is important to Canadians, and it has to do with the question of prices. We on this side of the House know that if it had not been for the Liberal government, the federal government would not have the power, through the Petroleum Administration Act, to establish prices, to establish a domestic price in Canada which is lower than the international price. If the Tory policy with respect to pricing were in place today, there would be no security for those in eastern Canada with respect to the kind of erratic price movements we are seeing, higher price movements being announced by the Middle East and the other supplying nations. There would be no security for Atlantic Canada with respect to price if it was not for the federal government's Petroleum Administration Act.

pany, Petro-Canada. That government did not say to me that it wanted its national oil company, Pemex, to work out the details with anybody else. It wants the deal made between the national oil company in Canada and the national oil company in Mexico. This is what security of supply is all about.

I am told as well that none of the provinces, when this bill went through the House the last time, raised any objections to provisions in the bill then, nor have they since. The last time this bill was in the House it received considerable discussion and attention, and I would hope, given the urgency of the situation outside this country-the revolution in Iran, the report of the mobilization of the armed forces of Saudi Arabia today, and the reports of the erratic price behaviour by the other OPEC producers, the unexpected increases-it will receive speedy passage. There is also the possibility that the United States may invoke rationing in the very near future. There are reports that the government of the United States has submitted legislation to Congress dealing with mandatory allocation measures and a rationing system.
Given these factors, and given the fact that Canada is a member by treaty of the emergency oil sharing arrangement under the International Energy Agency, whereby we would be obligated to invoke an allocation system in the event that world consumption were reduced as a result of shortage of supply by 7 per cent, and given the fact that we are 5 per cent already on a world-wide basis-which is not all that far away from the 7 per cent, the trigger level, as it is called-I would hope that the House and all parties would deal with this matter expeditiously so that we might deal with it in third reading form later this week.
