subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was just going to deal with the bill before us which, I think, confirms once again the move of this government to protect and serve more efficiently the interests of Canadians, a measure which hopefully will be supported by all Canadians. For this reason, the suggestion in Quebec now is that the Progressive Conservative party's greatest challenge is to find 60 candidates to cover the 75 constituencies in the province.
Mr. Speaker, Monday last I was giving enthusiastic support to Bill C-29 to amend the National Housing Act, thus highlighting the Canadian government's goal of using a new approach with other levels of government, a global approach under which three current projects, the neighbourhood improvement program, the municipal infrastructure program and the municipal incentive program would be merged into one, the community services grant program that would have an annual budget of about $150 million for 1980 and an expected $250 million for the next year, and if the various provinces so desire, further consultations could be opened to clarify certain technical points. If further improvements are desired, it will be perfectly possible to introduce them in later years, after those two years I referred to with financial commitments of roughly $150 and $250 million respectively.
This new approach stems from the requests of provincial governments wishing to assume fully that administrative responsibility which has been recognized by the Canadian government. The government will maintain its financial contributions along with other levels of government for the well-being of Canadians in order to improve the environment through better community services. The federal contribution will not be restricted to new housing or housing improvements, it will apply to the creation of community services extended by municipalities. Most importantly, this legislation has the flexibility needed. Municipalities that so desire can build community centres, or public parks, or public libraries, or they can improve municipal buildings.
Last Monday, I expressed my concerns with this new departure in social housing, based on the past performances of provincial governments. I referred to Canadian government commitments vis-a-vis the provinces in fiscal 1977. The Canadian government had allocated the provinces $353 million of public housing funds for people who need it most, people in the lowest income group. Of that amount, $199 million only were used in fiscal 1977.
Housing
One could denote at that time a little lack of enthusiasm on the part of provincial governments for the construction of public housing. But those worries might be set to rest because this bill does not put on the back burner non-profit organizations and housing corporations which will play an important role in the construction of housing for lower income people to help the Government of Canada reach the annual objective of
30,000	new housing units for low income people compared with the 19,000 now being built.
These are important amendments to the National Housing Act because non-profit organizations will be able to get financing from private organizations and lending institutions, and the Government of Canada will pitch in a special subsidy to reduce the interest rate, the commercial rate that can go from 11 per cent, 12 per cent or 13 per cent to 2 per cent. The subsidy will be paid annually by the Government of Canada to reduce interest rates and thus the liabilities of those.
Mr. Speaker, again I want to congratulate the ministers and the officers who played a major role in the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation because the end result, as I mentioned Monday, is very good. I think that result in the housing sector will also be reflected in the result we will get in the energy area. In the past four years 250,000 housing units were built in Canada. We can make a comparison because the Progressive Conservative party seems to go and get ideas from our American friends.
Here are our accomplishments in Canada during the years 1967 to 1977: on average ten new housing units were built in Canada per 1,000 population while during the same period the proportion in United States was only 6.8 for the same number of people. I think this indicates our housing policies were not all that bad. But there are also other comparisons which can be drawn to confirm once again that performance by the Government of Canada in recent years. I refer to the 1968 Gallup poll on housing. What were the results of that 1968 Gallup poll on housing? The results of that poll indicated that 60 per cent of people were satisfied with their housing, but 34 per cent were dissatisfied, and 6 per cent did not have an opinion.
Let us now look at the situation ten years later. Another Gallup poll was taken asking the same questions to ensure better continuity and easier comparison. Here are the results of this poll on housing taken at the end of 1978: 85 per cent of Canadians were satisfied with the housing situation and only 13 per cent were dissatisfied. This is a most positive result which confirms the extent to which the Trudeau government has applied itself to housing conditions in Canada, and I wish to take this opportunity to congratulate also those who contributed to this success. Of course, this success is due to the initiative of the government, through its ministers and members of parliament, but also to the assistance of the builders and all financial institutions.

February 28, 1979
Housing
This national success is also reflected in the various provinces. As I represent a city which now has a population of more than 250,000, I had a survey made to find out to what extent the federal housing authority had contributed to housing in Laval. The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation provided the following statistics on insured loans granted to home buyers in the city of Laval. From 1968 to 1977, authorized borrowers received $152,272,000 to build 7,279 units. Thanks to the direct loans granted under section 15, we were able to build 3,960 housing units for which financing amounted to $45 million.
Let us now look at the contribution of the Canadian government to the infrastructures in Laval. Once again, we find that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation made a major contribution to urban development, either through water purification projects, sewer systems or water systems, and I see here a figure of $8 million for 1976 alone. There is a contribution of $2 million for 1977, and I believe that in 1978, the amount of financing will exceed $8 million. In this case, we got about 25 per cent of the loan. So the Canadian government subsidizes home buyers and provides assistance at the municipal level for the construction of sewers and water pipes.
I asked how much money the Canadian government gave to the city of Laval for the construction of high-density units. Under his policy, the Canadian government gave $1,000 per unit. The policy ended last December. At that time, we provided a subsidy of a little over $2,158,000 for housing to reduce construction prices and thus to lower rents.
I have also a list of direct loans granted by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to construction companies building senior citizen homes for non-profit organizations.
The people of Laval, and I am convinced that the situation is the same in the ridings of my colleagues in this House, have built in Sainte-Rose a 174-unit senior citizen home entirely financed by the government of Canada. We have also built in Chomedey the Manoir Cardinal entirely financed by the government of Canada and three other homes financed in a proportion of 90 to 95 per cent, by the Quebec Housing Corporation, the Manoir des ties, the Residence Sainte-Doro-thee, and we are building two other homes eligible for subsidies from the Quebec Housing Corporation, but which are financed at 95 per cent by the government of Canada, one in Laval-des-Rapides and another in Chomedey which will accommodate about 200 people and be financed by both governments. Mr. Speaker, those are some of the projects undertaken in co-operation with the provincial government and with extensive help from the municipalities.
Mr. Speaker, I quoted those figures to emphasize the role played by the Government of Canada, through the National Housing Act, in the housing field. And to support my argument, I refer to an article from La Presse dated February 20, about a report published in the magazine Habitation 79 on the comparative purchasing cost of a single family house in

Ontario, in Laval and in Western Ontario, in Metropolitan Toronto, at Mississauga. The cost of land is $12,692 in Toronto, $2,400 in Laval, and they mentioned also the cost of local services and I wish to underline that there are some differences, that the legislation is different as public services are not financed in the same way in the province of Quebec as in the province of Ontario. In fact municipalities in Quebec pay for the services, that is sewer and water systems and sidewalks, through municipal taxes, while in Ontario, when you buy a lot these services are financed by the promoters. So the cost of these services is included in the price of the land and the owners pay only a property tax.
Notwithstanding all this, Mr. Speaker, I can say that we have contributed to lower building costs by giving assistance to developers, by financially helping municipalities and by creating this competition between promoters. I am sure that a property which costs $35,910 to build in Laval, as mentioned in the article, would cost about $65,000 in Ontario, in greater Toronto, because of the reasons I mentioned and because of the different tax structure.
Thanks to the initiative taken by the Canadian government in putting programs at the disposal of all agencies having a direct interest in housing, we have succeeded in reducing housing construction costs in Canada as a whole and in Quebec in particular. I feel that if there had been more landowners in Toronto, a little more competition between landowners or developers, they would have obtained for home buyers the same benefits as in Quebec.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I hope that opposition members are as conscious as we are on this side of the House of the importance this legislation has both for those who want better housing conditions and for the municipalities which will use the funds available under this legislation to provide their residents with parks, libraries and the infrastructure required.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on Bill C-29, which is designed to amend the National Housing Act and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act and to make other related amendments. Shelter, Mr. Speaker, is one of the most basic human needs and has been so from time immemorial. Shelter, whether it be in the form of modern housing or any other suitable form to protect human beings against adverse elements of nature, has always been regarded as a criterion for measuring the quality of life.
I am, therefore, glad to speak on a matter such as housing, that is so close to all of us and fundamental to the well-being of any society. This debate on amending the National Housing Act affords some of us on this side of the House the welcome opportunity to make a contribution and offer our opinion on the national housing policy.
February 28, 1979

It has been a most frustrating experience, to say the least, to have to put up with the stonewalling tactics of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) during his appearances before the housing committee. On occasion the minister would disallow members of this department from answering members' queries and legitimate concern about the direction of housing policy. Maybe the government has no housing policy and is therefore unable to be answerable to Canadians about its haphazard programs.
You will recall that the proposals contained in the bill now before the House were First made public almost a year ago. Given the minister's pomposity, and propensity to election jitters, he readily pounces on the opportunity to make unrealistic promise-filled pronouncements. At this stage, however, the hide and seek game is over, and the government will have to face the Canadian electorate and account for its bankupt policies.
I would like to address myself to the residential rehabilitation program, which was introduced to provide federal aid in the improvement and repair of substandard dwellings. The Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program is one of the four major areas to be affected by the bill now before us. Under the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, RRAP, loans, part of which could be forgiven, were available only to homeowners and landlords who owned property in neighbourhood improvement areas of the country, and for non-profit housing projects. The new legislation intends to remove these restrictions and allow RRAP to be applicable on a universal basis.
Now coming to the universal application of the rehabilitation program, the proposal to remove any restraints on the applicability of the program is the greatest deception of all. Previously RRAP funds were only available to houses located within neighbourhood improvement areas, so designated in conjunction with provincial and local governments. An internal memo from Mr. Hession, the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, to the minister states:
You realize I am sure that neither the industry not the municipal delivery system nor the present and projected RRAP budget permit the operation of a "universal" program . . . Rehabilitation effort will continue to be concentrated in specified action areas as in the past, but as a matter of policy, not formal legislation.
In view of this apparent contradiction between the terms outlined in the bill as to the universal application of RRAP and the advice from the department to the effect that the pursuit of such a policy is not feasible at this time, is the minister's statement just another election inspired promise, obviously never to be fulfilled? Has the minister undertaken serious consultations with his department officials to determine what course of action to follow, or is the minister posturing for the up-coming election?
The internal memo to which I referred cautions the minister against making promises that the department knows it cannot fulfil. It states, for instance, .. we should avoid raising expectations which we cannot satisfy." The hon. gentleman
Housing
would be well advised to heed the sound advice of his departmental officials instead of making promises that he knows himself he cannot fulfil. He ought to consider his own department's ten-year plan to modernize and rehabilitate Canada's housing stock.
It is estimated there are approximately two million housing units in Canada which were constructed prior to the end of the Second World War. These premises are in dire need of modernization, whether simply to upgrade insulation or to carry out repairs on the basic structures. I support the contention of CMHC that over a ten-year period the 200,000 to 400,000 dwellings in need of serious upgrading, which are occupied by lower income people, should be brought up to maintenance and occupancy standards with RRAP funds. It is important to establish fair criteria to determine those who are in greatest need of funds for rehabilitation, and to this end I strongly urge that the program be made universal. Adequate and appropriate criteria should be developed to process applications. At the present time 20,000 units are being rehabilitated annually.
While the minister amuses himself playing number games to content himself with the achievements of the department, countless Canadians are joining the list of perplexed victims of the government's erratic housing policies. If there is a single word that sums up the policies of the federal government in housing, that word is "erratic". The minister is preoccupied with politicizing the housing issue rather than spending his time and energies devising means to help achieve a better standard of living for Canadians.
We cannot afford to look upon programs such as RRAP in isolation. They tie in with the mainstream of economic life in our nation. For instance, expansion of the rehabilitation program would undoubtedly offer employment to a large number of Canadians, and the spin-off effect would be felt in various other supporting industries. This would be a much welcomed move in view of the present high rate of unemployment in the construction industry.
While welcoming the move up the socio-economic ladder of many Canadians who have become homeowners of late, I cannot but help express sympathy with many unfortunate individuals who have had to give up their homes. The federal government programs lured many of these individuals into home ownership on grounds and terms which were not fair to prospective owners.
In 1978 the first home owners under the Assisted Home Ownership Program-AHOP-saw their five-year subsidy come to an end. The results have been extremely disappointing in that 10 per cent defaulted on their mortgages, unable or unwilling to meet their payments. This compares, by the way, with a default rate of only one half of one per cent on regular mortgages. It is in this area that the minister lacks compassion and sensitivity to the plight of home owners. He is merely interested in playing a numbers game to support his theory that no other person or government can do better than his own.
To support the point I am making, Mr. Speaker, a study done in 1972 by three faculty members of the University of Montreal charged that CMHC was too close to the develop-

February 28, 1979
Housing
ment industry and was more concerned with housing starts than with the type of quality of housing needed. A case in point is the career of a well-known developer who turned administrator and then back to developer. I refer, of course, to the person of Mr. Teron, now in private business at the expense of the public purse.
In discussing the bill before us, may I take the opportunity to register concern over the federal government's unwillingness to contract out work to non-union labour? This leaves a number of small though reliable firms out in the cold when it comes to securing government contracts. I have spoken before in favour of allocating as many federal government projects to small businesses as possible. In view of the importance of this sector to our economy, I urge the government to give every encouragement to the small scale construction firms in the housing industry.
I have been an advocate of free market forces of supply and demand being the determining factor in the running of our economy. After all, it is on that that our economic success is modelled. I strongly suggest that the federal government allow the forces of the free market system to determine the price structure in the housing industry. Evidence all around us from various countries should convince anyone that, when market forces are allowed to operate freely the end product is more often than not less costly than when there is heavy government intervention.
Sometimes the cost of administering government programs is prohibitive and is detrimental to the very success of the
programs. For instance, the government is still baffled about the lack of response to the Canadian home insulation program. Without elaborating at any great length, I would make the brief observation that the government ought to engage in a more vigorous advertising campaign to inform Canadians about the program. As well, the federal government might reconsider the present terms of the program. Most of us are aware that there is a special grant of $500 available in only two of the provinces, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. This $500 represents an outright grant.
I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that there are frigid zones elsewhere, including my own riding of Parry Sound-Muskoka, where insulation is even more badly needed than in those areas. Further, I would point out that the $500 grant available in the rest of Canada is subject to income tax. It is all well and good for a person whose income is so low that he does not have to pay income tax, but I repeat, in my view these arrangements are discriminatory. Again, the grant pays only two-thirds of the cost of materials up to $500. Of course if you purchase more than $500 worth of insulation materials you would be able to secure the full amount.
May I call it six o'clock?
